_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: If so: that Rabbi Shimon’s reason is a matter of benefit [what may not be used for benefit cannot be fed to others, and so is not called food].
gershom:a1.1: If so: according to Rabbi Shimon, why specifically [say] that meat in milk becomes impure with the impurity of food because it had a period of fitness? Derive that it becomes impure because it is food you can feed to others, to gentiles, since he holds it is permitted for benefit, as Rabbi Shimon [ben Yehuda] teaches, etc.
rashi:a2.1: Just as there, it is permitted for benefit: as it is written, “You shall cast it to the dogs” (Exodus 22:30).
tosafot:a2.1: In brief: Just as there it is forbidden for eating and permitted for benefit: this is puzzling, since in the chapter Kol Sha’ah (Pesaḥim 24b) Isi ben Yehuda derives the prohibition of eating [meat in milk] from here and derives the prohibition of benefit by an a fortiori inference from orla. So in what do they disagree? One may answer that the tanna there holds that since both can be upheld, the verbal analogy and the a fortiori inference both stand. But this is still difficult, since in many places a verbal analogy comes and overrides an a fortiori inference (“I might have thought… and make an a fortiori inference… the verse states”). Rabbeinu Tam explained: [for the tanna there] the verse also speaks of something forbidden for benefit, such as consecrated meat that left its boundary, as is expounded from “flesh in the field” in the chapter Behema HaMakshah (Ḥullin 68a); so although the plain sense of the verse is that benefit is permitted (“You shall cast it to the dogs”), the a fortiori inference has a purpose, deriving from consecrated meat, which the verse also covers. The tanna here derives from a tereifa, which is permitted for benefit according to the plain sense, and does not accept the a fortiori inference, just as the one who derives the prohibition of benefit from the three times “you shall not cook” does not accept it. And why not derive the prohibition of benefit from “it shall be burned in fire… because it is holy,” as disqualified consecrated items are derived from it in Kol Sha’ah (Pesaḥim 24a)? One may answer that “a holy people” and “holy men” are of one subject and resemble each other; alternatively, one derives non-sacred matters from non-sacred matters and not non-sacred matters from consecrated ones, as is said in the chapter Kisui HaDam (Ḥullin 85a). Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:a3.1: For him too: for the Jew himself it had a period of fitness. But an ox that is stoned and a heifer whose neck is broken never had a period of fitness, even beforehand, since an animal in its lifetime stands in a presumption of prohibition [it may not be eaten until it is slaughtered].
rashi:a4.1: Let it teach: “And Rabbi Shimon concedes with regard to a firstborn donkey”: since it is food he can feed to others.
gershom:a2.1: And moreover, for him too, for a Jew, it had a period of fitness before it was cooked in milk. And if it is so that after the breaking of its neck it is permitted for benefit according to Rabbi Shimon, let it teach: “And Rabbi Shimon concedes regarding a firstborn donkey and meat in milk that they become impure with the impurity of food,” since both are permitted for benefit and are food you can feed to others. Rather, since it does not teach “and he concedes regarding a firstborn donkey,” learn from it that after the breaking of its neck it is forbidden.
gershom:a3.1: Actually Rabbi Shimon permits it for benefit; and why does it not become impure with the impurity of food?
rashi:a5.1: Where he did not intend it: for eating. And that is why it is not taught [as an exception], since ordinarily it does not stand to be eaten.
gershom:a4.1: Here we are dealing with where he did not intend it at the time of breaking its neck, so that it would become impure with the impurity of food.
rashi:a6.1: Since its prohibition is its intent: the prohibition with which the Merciful One forbade it to a Jew makes it food; since He forbade it, it follows that it is fit to be eaten by a gentile.
gershom:a5.1: The Sages said it before Rav Sheshet: that is why, according to the Rabbis, it becomes impure with the impurity of food: since a donkey is forbidden to a Jew for eating, the stringency of its prohibition is its intent, to become impure with the impurity of food.
gershom:a6.1: And Rabbi Shimon does not say its prohibition is its intent; rather, if he intended it, it becomes impure with the impurity of food, and if not, not.
rashi:a7.1: It requires intent: to become impure with the impurity of food if a creeping animal touched it, so that if it then touches fit food it renders that food impure. As long as one has not intended it [for eating], it has no impurity of contact at all, since the carcass of a kosher bird imparts impurity only when one eats it, and then it renders impure the garments he is wearing at the time of swallowing.
rashi:a7.2: And it does not require being rendered susceptible: since it carries a severe impurity, rendering a person and garments impure if he eats it. And it is said in Keritot, in the chapter Dam Sheḥita (Keritot 21a): [the verse] “And if water is put [on seed]” etc.: just as seeds are distinguished in that they will not in the end impart a severe impurity, and they require being rendered susceptible, so too anything that will not in the end impart a severe impurity requires being rendered susceptible. And being rendered susceptible applies only to the light impurity of foods; and so too intent.
gershom:a7.1: And according to the Rabbis, do we say, etc.? But we learned in Tractate Okatzin [so Rabbeinu Gershom; the Davidson English cites Teharot 1:1]: thirteen matters were said concerning the carcass of a kosher bird, and this is one of them: it requires intent and does not require being rendered susceptible. That is, it becomes impure with the impurity of food only if he intended it to be eaten by a gentile. It requires intent because it has no other impurity: the carcass of a bird does not impart impurity by touching an olive’s bulk, like the carcass of an animal, but only by eating, in the throat. Therefore it requires intent to become impure with the impurity of food with an egg’s bulk. And it does not require being rendered susceptible by water: even without water, if a creeping animal touched an egg’s bulk of the bird carcass, it becomes impure. Why does it not require it? Because we hold that whatever will in the end impart a severe impurity with an olive’s bulk does not require being rendered susceptible, and this bird carcass too, when one eats an olive’s bulk of it, renders garments impure in the throat, and that is a severe impurity with an olive’s bulk, like an animal carcass; but an animal carcass imparts impurity by touching an olive’s bulk, without eating. And it mentions a kosher bird as requiring intent, though all the more so the carcass of a non-kosher bird, to teach a novelty: even though a kosher bird is fit to eat for both a Jew and a gentile, even so its carcass becomes impure with the impurity of food only with intent. And if you say “its prohibition is its intent,” that since it is forbidden to a Jew for eating it is significant, and it is fit for a gentile to eat, so it should become impure with the impurity of food, why do I need further intent?
rashi:a8.1: It is Rabbi Shimon: who does not hold that its prohibition is its intent.
gershom:a8.1: Who is this, that requires intent? It is Rabbi Shimon, who does not hold its prohibition is its intent.
rashi:a9.1: The carcass of a non-kosher animal in any location: since ordinarily it does not stand to be eaten, as it is repulsive; and moreover it has two disqualifications: one, that it was not slaughtered, and one, that it is non-kosher. And so too the carcass of a kosher bird.
rashi:a9.2: And the fat: the fat of a kosher animal’s carcass.
rashi:a9.3: In the villages: since they are poor and not accustomed to eating fowl and fat, these require intent to feed them to a gentile; otherwise they do not become impure with the impurity of food. And if you ask: why does the carcass of a non-kosher animal need the impurity of food, when it renders people and vessels impure, and all the more so foods? Answer as is said in Keritot, in the chapter Dam Sheḥita (Keritot 21a): where there is less than an olive’s bulk of it, it carries no carcass impurity, since it lacks the measure, and they joined it to less than an egg’s bulk of food: if he intended this less-than-an-olive’s-bulk for eating, it combines with the other food to complete an egg’s bulk, so that if a creeping animal touches them they become impure. And “the fat” we do not read [in this clause], since one cannot say of it that it does not require being rendered susceptible. If it is the fat of a carcass, it does not impart a severe impurity, as it is written, “It may be used for any other work” (Leviticus 7:24), so why should it not require being rendered susceptible? And if it is of a slaughtered animal, and [the reason is] that it was already rendered susceptible, we learned in the Gemara of Ha’Or VeHarotev (Ḥullin 128a): Rabbi Akiva retracted and taught in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, that the susceptibility given by slaughter does not help for fat, since it is not yet food, for the fat of the villages is not food until one intends it. And in [the order of] Teharot, in the mishna, we do not read it.
rashi:a9.4: And it does not require being rendered susceptible: since it imparted a severe impurity while there was a whole olive’s bulk of it, while it was still attached to the carcass.
tosafot:a9.1: The carcass of a non-kosher animal in any location, and the carcass of a kosher bird in the villages, require intent and do not require being rendered susceptible: [Tosafot quote Rashi:] “And ‘the fat’ we do not read, since one cannot say it does not require being rendered susceptible: if it is the fat of a carcass, it does not impart a severe impurity, as it is written, ‘It may be used for any other work’ (Leviticus 7:24), so why should it not require being rendered susceptible? And if it is of a slaughtered animal, we learned in Ha’Or VeHarotev (Ḥullin 128a): Rabbi Akiva retracted and taught in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda that the susceptibility given by slaughter does not help for fat, since it is not yet food, for in the villages it is not food until one intends it. And in Tractate Teharot we do not read it.” End of his words. [Tosafot quote it in full] because there are copies of the commentary in which it is not written, and perhaps it was added by others. And although Rav Pappa there (Ḥullin 128a) explains the tannaitic dispute as concerning what intent permits, in any case it is reasonable that the unattributed mishna in Tractate Teharot follows the retraction. And in the latter clause we properly read “the fat in the marketplaces requires neither intent nor being rendered susceptible,” and we say it of the fat of a slaughtered animal; and so the Kuntres [Rashi] explained.
tosafot:a9.2: And the carcass of a kosher bird in the villages: the Kuntres [Rashi] explained that they are poor and not accustomed to eating fowl. It seems right to explain another reason: in the marketplaces there are many eaters, and they buy everything; in the villages there are few eaters, and they buy only choice things.
gershom:a9.1: Come and hear: the carcass of a non-kosher animal in any location: whether in the villages or the cities, where both poor and rich are accustomed to eat; even so it requires intent with regard to the impurity of food. Why does it require intent? Because it is a non-kosher animal, which was not fit for a Jew to eat. And this requirement of intent is not for the carcass itself to become impure with the impurity of food with an egg’s bulk, since it is itself impure with a severe impurity with an olive’s bulk without intent. Rather, it requires intent to combine: for example, where there is less than an egg’s bulk of other food that is not of the carcass, and there is less than an olive’s bulk of these [the text adds “the offspring of a non-kosher animal”], which combines with that food and makes it an egg’s bulk. And that less-than-an-olive’s-bulk, since it lacks the measure of severe impurity, has no impurity in itself and can combine for the impurity of food; therefore it requires intent. And the carcass of a kosher bird: even though a kosher bird is fit for both a Jew and a gentile, since in the villages they are not accustomed to eat fowl, it requires intent. And for the impurity of food of a bird nothing is needed to combine; it speaks of an egg’s bulk of the bird carcass itself. And it does not require being rendered susceptible, for even without it it imparts impurity, since we said that whatever will in the end impart a severe impurity does not require being rendered susceptible; rather, if a creeping animal touched them without their being rendered susceptible, they become impure with the impurity of food. And here we do not say its prohibition is its intent.
gershom:a10.1: Who is this? It is Rabbi Shimon.
rashi:a10.1: The carcass of a kosher animal in any location: ordinarily it stands to be eaten by a gentile, since it is not repulsive; and moreover, for a Jew it has only one disqualification. Therefore it does not require intent to receive the impurity of food, so that less than an olive’s bulk of it combines with less than an egg’s bulk of food. And so too the carcass of a kosher bird, and the fat of a slaughtered animal.
rashi:a10.2: In the marketplaces: in the large towns, where there are many people and they are wealthy and accustomed to eating plenty of fowl and fat.
rashi:a10.3: Nor being rendered susceptible: the carcass of an animal or a bird, because they impart a severe impurity; and the fat of a slaughtered animal in the marketplaces, because it was already rendered susceptible by the slaughter. Since it does not require intent, the susceptibility given by slaughter works for it.
tosafot:a10.1: The carcass of a kosher animal in any location: as for the distinction between a non-kosher and a kosher animal: even though both are sold only to a gentile, and [gentiles] prefer the pig, as we say there (Ḥullin 17a) on “And houses full of all good things”: [necks] of pigs, and we say in Megilla (13a) on “And he advanced her to the best”: [necks] of pigs, even so, being kosher makes it food even when it is only slightly fit, since when it is not a carcass it is full food for a Jew. And for this reason, for Rabbi Shimon, the kosher signs of the camel, hare, rock badger and pig help to make them food, as is said shortly. And the Kuntres [Rashi] also explained here: the carcass of a non-kosher animal in any location ordinarily does not stand to be eaten, as it is repulsive, and moreover it has two disqualifications, one that it was not slaughtered and one that it is non-kosher; and of the carcass of a kosher animal he explained that it ordinarily stands to be eaten by a gentile, since it is not repulsive, and moreover for a Jew it has only one disqualification; therefore it does not require intent.
tosafot:a10.2: And the fat in the marketplaces: Rashi explained, “they are accustomed to eating fowl and fat [shuman].” This implies that he means that all fat is called ḥelev here, and it does not speak specifically of forbidden fat, such as the fat lying under a membrane that peels off (Ḥullin 49b).
gershom:a11.1: Come and hear: the carcass of a kosher animal in any location, since it was fit for both a Jew and a gentile; and the carcass of a kosher bird and the fat in the marketplaces: “in the marketplaces” means in the cities, which are places of marketplaces, for there they are accustomed to eat both fowl and fat, since they are wealthy. But villagers are not accustomed to eat either fowl or fat, for they keep the fat for a lamp, to do their work by its light. Therefore the carcass of a kosher animal in any location, and the carcass of a kosher bird and the fat in the marketplaces, that is, in the cities, require no intent, for without intent they become impure with the impurity of food; nor being rendered susceptible, as we said. It follows that a non-kosher animal in any location requires intent, since it was not fit for both a Jew and a gentile, and we do not say its prohibition is its intent.
rashi:a10.4: But a non-kosher one requires intent: and we do not say its prohibition is its intent.
rashi:a11.1: Even the camel: its law is like that of a kosher animal, since it has one of the signs of a kosher animal. And since Rabbi Shimon adds this in the latter clause, it follows that the first clause is the Rabbis’, and learn from it that they do not hold its prohibition is its intent. And regarding the firstborn donkey, which [the Rabbis] deem impure above, that is where he intended it [for eating], and even so Rabbi Shimon deems it pure, since it is food that you cannot feed to others, for Rabbi Shimon concedes that after the breaking of its neck it is forbidden, in accordance with Rabba [Rashi abbreviates the name].
gershom:a12.1: And if you say: who is this, that requires intent? It is Rabbi Shimon, who does not hold its prohibition is its intent. But since the latter clause is Rabbi Shimon, etc. What is the reason? Since they have a sign of a kosher animal, they are significant like the carcass of a kosher animal.
gershom:a13.1: It follows that the first clause is not Rabbi Shimon but the Rabbis, and we infer: but a non-kosher one requires intent. Evidently the Rabbis do not hold its prohibition is its intent.
rashi:a12.1: Rather, Rava says: everyone agrees we do not say “its prohibition is its intent”: by itself. And even so their dispute is where he did not intend it, and the statement of Rabba [abbreviated] is not upheld. And as for your difficulty, what is the reason of the Rabbis: if he broke its neck, so too the Rabbis concede that it does not become impure with the impurity of food, since he did not intend it.
gershom:a14.1: Rather, Rava says: everyone, both Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis, agrees we do not say its prohibition is its intent. And if you say: neither for the firstborn donkey nor for these, why do they not require full intent? [A gloss in the printed text suggests the reading should be: “and if he broke its neck, so too,” or “if he slaughtered it,” etc.] Or if he slaughtered it plainly, without intent, its slaughter is its intent, to become impure with the impurity of food. And actually the statement of Rabba, who said Rabbi Shimon concedes it is forbidden after the breaking of its neck, is not upheld; rather, after the breaking of its neck too Rabbi Shimon permits it in these. And if you say: if so, for Rabbi Shimon, since after the breaking of its neck it is permitted for benefit, it is food you can feed to others, so let it also teach, “Rabbi Shimon concedes regarding a firstborn donkey and meat in milk,” etc.: certainly, where he broke the neck of this firstborn donkey, so too for Rabbi Shimon it becomes impure with the impurity of food, since breaking the neck is like a plain slaughter: just as a plain slaughter does not require intent, since its slaughter is its intent, so too its neck-breaking is its intent, to become impure with the impurity of food, according to all.
rashi:b1.1: Here we are dealing with where he slaughtered it: the firstborn donkey. If he slaughtered it as a full slaughter, even according to Rabbi Shimon it counts as intent and it becomes impure. Rather, where he slaughtered it in order to learn the laws of slaughter by it; and this is their dispute: the Rabbis hold that this slaughter makes it food like a proper, full slaughter, as we say in Ha’Or VeHarotev (Ḥullin 117b), “One who slaughters an animal for a gentile…,” as I explained above; and Rabbi Shimon holds that this slaughter is not a proper one and does not count as intent. And [they disagree] in the dispute of Nimos and Rabbi Eliezer.
gershom:b1.1: Rather, here we are dealing with: why does it not become impure with the impurity of food according to Rabbi Shimon? Where he slaughtered this firstborn donkey to learn the laws of slaughter by it, and not for eating. This slaughter to learn is inferior to breaking the neck and to a plain slaughter; therefore Rabbi Shimon holds it does not become impure with the impurity of food, and the Rabbis hold that it counts as its intent, since he intended a slaughter of some kind.
rashi:b2.1: Its blood renders susceptible: if it fell on produce. And all the more so if he slaughtered it with a full slaughter, its blood renders susceptible, even for [the crow] itself, since its slaughter is its intent. And if he stabbed it and did not slaughter it, Rabbi Eliezer would no longer disagree, for certainly its blood renders others susceptible, but not [the crow] itself, since it does not itself receive impurity without intent.
tosafot:b2.1: That one who slaughters a crow to learn, its blood renders susceptible: the Kuntres [Rashi] explained: “if it fell on produce; and all the more so if he slaughtered it with a full slaughter, its blood renders susceptible even for itself, since its slaughter is its intent; and if he stabbed it and did not slaughter it, Rabbi Eliezer would no longer disagree, for certainly its blood renders others susceptible, but not itself, since it does not itself receive impurity without intent.” End of his words. It is puzzling that he explained that the blood of stabbing renders others susceptible: for what reason would it do so, since it is not blood of slaughter, and [the category of] blood of the slain applies not to an animal but only to a person?
rashi:b3.1: Rather, is it not “its prohibition is its intent”: together with the slaughter, in such a case, that is between them.
gershom:b2.1: And in the dispute: Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis disagree in the dispute of Sumkhos [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the Gemara reads Nimos] and Rabbi Eliezer, as it is taught: Rabbi Yosei said, etc. But Rabbi Eliezer is the same as the first tanna! Rather, is it not “its prohibition is its intent” that is between them? This “its prohibition is its intent” is not like the “its prohibition is its intent” above, for if it were the same, it would be difficult for Rava, who said everyone agrees we do not say its prohibition is its intent. Rather, by “its prohibition is its intent” here it means a slaughter to learn, which is not a proper slaughter for eating; that is what it calls “its prohibition.”
rashi:b4.1: For others: if it fell on produce. But for itself it requires intent, since we do not say mere “its prohibition is its intent,” and this slaughter is not significant enough to make it food.
gershom:b3.1: The first tanna holds its blood renders susceptible for others: for all other foods, so that if a creeping animal touched them they are susceptible to impurity even without intent. But for itself, the crow’s flesh, even though it is certainly rendered susceptible by its blood, it becomes impure only with intent, since we do not say of slaughter that its prohibition is its intent.
rashi:b5.1: And even for itself it does not require intent: since this slaughter makes it food. And in this too the Rabbis hold like Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Shimon like Nimos.
gershom:b4.1: And Rabbi Eliezer comes to say that the blood of slaughter, whether of a full slaughter or of a slaughter to learn, always renders susceptible, so that even for itself no further intent is needed; rather, “its prohibition,” a slaughter to learn, is also its intent. And the Rabbis, who hold that the firstborn donkey becomes impure, hold like Rabbi Eliezer; and Rabbi Shimon, who said that the firstborn donkey does not become impure, holds like the first tanna, that a slaughter to learn is not its intent for impurity. And this is “in the dispute.”
rashi:b6.1: Since it has signs of a kosher bird: as is said in Elu Tereifot (Ḥullin 61b). That is why it is food. But regarding a firstborn donkey, which has no signs of a kosher animal, had he not intended it, the Rabbis would not deem it impure on account of this slaughter. And Rabbi Shimon, even though he intended it, disagrees, since it is forbidden for benefit after the breaking of its neck, in accordance with Rabba [abbreviated].
tosafot:b6.1: A crow is different, since it has signs of a kosher bird: the same applies to [all] twenty-four [non-kosher] birds except the nesher, as is evident in the chapter Elu Tereifot (Ḥullin 61b).
gershom:b5.1: From where? Perhaps actually we cannot say that the Rabbis hold like Rabbi Eliezer, for as to the reason of Rabbi Eliezer, why he says the blood of slaughter always renders susceptible, even [a slaughter] to learn: perhaps a crow is different, for regarding a crow he holds so because it has a kosher sign, as we say in Shechitat Chullin: “to include the amki crow, which has a crop.” But regarding a firstborn donkey, which has no kosher sign, he would never hold that a slaughter to learn is its intent. And then whom do the Rabbis follow? Neither Rabbi Eliezer nor Nimos.
rashi:b7.1: And from where do we derive that signs of a kosher animal are a significant matter: to bring it to impurity: as is taught about it in the baraita above, “The carcass of a kosher animal…”
gershom:b6.1: And from where do we derive that a kosher sign is a significant matter, as we said, perhaps Rabbi Eliezer’s reason is that a crow is different, etc.? As is taught about that baraita: Rabbi Shimon said, etc. And if you say: if the reason is a kosher sign, why does Rabbi Eliezer specify one who slaughters to learn? Let him say even one who slaughters unawares, for unawares is worse than to learn; unawares is, for example, where he meant to cut something else and cut [the throat] without intending to; and even so it would teach us that the blood of slaughter in any case always renders susceptible, since it has a kosher sign. So why does he specify to learn?
rashi:b8.1: Even unawares: intending to cut something else, not intending slaughter.
tosafot:b8.1: Why specifically to learn? Even unawares: that is, and even if he stabbed it, for slaughtering unawares is also not slaughter, and it is like stabbing. And although then it would not have been rendered susceptible by the blood of slaughter, in any case [the Gemara] asks, since [Rabbi Eliezer] does not come to teach us that the blood of slaughter renders susceptible, for that we were already taught; he comes only to teach us that it does not require intent since it has signs of a kosher bird, and this he could have taught us without slaughter.
rashi:b8.2: Yes, this is indeed so, and because of Nimos: to make known the strength [of Nimos’s view]: even though he slaughtered it to learn, which is a more significant slaughter than one done unawares, even so Nimos does not deem [the crow] itself impure.
gershom:b7.1: Yes, this is indeed so: that is, according to Rabbi Eliezer the same applies to slaughter unawares, which also always renders susceptible, since it has a kosher sign. And why did he specify to learn? Because of Nimos: for Nimos, if one slaughtered to learn, its blood renders susceptible, but unawares its blood does not, since he does not consider it slaughter. And still you cannot establish the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis as the dispute of Nimos and Rabbi Eliezer, since we say perhaps a crow is different, etc. Rather, perforce you must establish that they disagree about actual neck-breaking, and actually in accordance with Rabba, who said Rabbi Shimon concedes that after neck-breaking it is forbidden. The reason of the Rabbis, who say it becomes impure with the impurity of food, is that its neck-breaking is its intent; and Rabbi Shimon holds that even though its neck-breaking is its intent, since he holds that after neck-breaking it is forbidden for benefit, it is food you cannot feed to others, and therefore it does not become impure with the impurity of food.
rashi:b9.1: He raised an objection: Abaye to Rava, who said Rabbi Shimon concedes after the breaking of its neck. [Rashi names Rava as the author of this ruling; the Davidson English, with the printed text of 9b, gives the ruling to Rabba and the proof to Rava.]
rashi:b9.2: With a cleaver: a large knife, since that is the manner of breaking the neck.
rashi:b9.3: From behind: opposite the nape of its neck [oref], as it is written, “And you shall break its neck [va’arafto].”
gershom:b8.1: Abaye raised an objection to Rava: if he did not want to redeem it, he breaks its neck with a cleaver from behind, at its nape. [Rabbeinu Gershom too names Abaye and Rava; the Davidson English says the Gemara objects to the opinion of Rabba.]
gershom:b9.1: Say: that is, resolve the baraita and read it thus: “and buries it,” and while alive a firstborn donkey is forbidden for benefit, and Rabbi Shimon permits; but after neck-breaking he concedes it is forbidden, as I said.
gershom:b10.1: But since the latter clause is about while alive, etc.: “and it is forbidden for shearing and labor,” which is while alive.
rashi:b12.1: With a saw [megeira]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss) a knife with many notches.
rashi:b13.1: With benefit from its value: if he rented it out to others.
gershom:b11.1: Both the first clause and the latter clause are about while alive: the first clause, which teaches “and it is forbidden for benefit,” speaks of benefit from its value, that if he sold it or rented it out, its proceeds are forbidden; and the latter clause, which says it is forbidden for shearing and labor, is benefit from its body.
rashi:b14.1: With benefit from its body: such as shearing and labor.
gershom:b12.1: And it was necessary [to teach both], for had it taught, etc. And actually after neck-breaking Rabbi Shimon concedes that it is forbidden, in accordance with Rabba.
rashi:b18.1: Just as redemption permits: for after its redemption all agree it is permitted for benefit.
gershom:b13.1: Just as redemption permits the firstborn donkey for benefit, so too neck-breaking would permit benefit, and it would be permitted after neck-breaking even according to Rabbi Yehuda; [the verse] teaches us that it is not.
rashi:b19.1: He caused a loss of the priest’s money: in that he did not redeem it with a lamb and give it to the priest.
rashi:b19.2: Therefore his money shall be lost: the court compels him to break its neck after thirty [days], as is explained in the chapter, and it is forbidden for benefit.
gershom:b14.1: He caused a loss of the priest’s money: in that he did not want to give him a lamb as its redemption, which the Omnipresent would grant him; therefore his money shall be lost, in that he breaks its neck and does not benefit from it.
rashi:b20.1: It is already lost: since it is forbidden for benefit even while alive, what does breaking its neck cost him?
rashi:b20.2: Rather, is it not Rabbi Shimon: and he concedes after the breaking of its neck.
gershom:b15.1: Whose is this? If we say Rabbi Yehuda, it is already lost, for he forbids it for benefit even while alive, before redemption.
gershom:b16.1: Rather, is it not Rabbi Shimon? Evidently he holds that after neck-breaking it is forbidden for benefit. No; actually nothing can be learned from this. Even so, you could resolve this teaching of Levi: if you wish, say Rabbi Shimon, and if you wish, say Rabbi Yehuda. If you wish, say Rabbi Shimon, who permits benefit both while it is alive and after neck-breaking; and what is the “his money shall be lost” that it says? Not to forbid it for benefit; rather, it speaks of the depreciation of death: now that he has broken its neck, its value has dropped far below what it was worth alive, and that is “his money shall be lost.” But in any case it is permitted for benefit after neck-breaking.
rashi:b22.1: The difference [beinei beinei]: since it is forbidden for benefit even while alive, he could have redeemed it with a lamb worth a danka [a small coin], and now he loses everything.
gershom:b17.1: And if you wish, say Rabbi Yehuda: what is the “his money shall be lost” that it says? The loss of the difference: that is, with a lamb worth a danka he could have redeemed a firstborn donkey worth a sela and gained that difference, by which the donkey is worth more than the lamb, and after redemption it would be permitted for benefit; and now, when he breaks its neck, he loses it.
rashi:b23.1: Or if you wish, say Rabbi Shimon: and even so it does not become forbidden for benefit. And how did he lose his money? By the depreciation of death: what death took off its value, for alive it was worth a maneh, and after death it is worth only a dinar, to feed to his dog.
rashi:b25.1: This of Rav Naḥman: who said above that Rabbi Shimon concedes after the breaking of its neck.
gershom:b18.1: There are those who teach this of Rav Naḥman on this: that is, Rav Naḥman did not say it as a general statement, “And similarly Rav Naḥman said,” but Rav Naḥman said it on this: one who betroths with a firstborn donkey, after neck-breaking, and all agree, for even Rabbi Shimon concedes that it is forbidden for benefit, and she is not betrothed.
rashi:b26.1: She should be betrothed with all of it: since all of it is permitted for benefit.
gershom:b19.1: If Rabbi Shimon, she should be betrothed with all of it: the firstborn donkey, since he permits it for benefit.
gershom:b20.1: And if Rabbi Yehuda, she should be betrothed with that difference: that is, since she can redeem a donkey worth a shekel with a lamb worth a danka, let her be betrothed with that difference.
rashi:b27.1: That is worth only a shekel: a sela. For now there is no difference, since the lamb we give the priest in its place must be worth a shekel.
gershom:b21.1: Rabba said [the Davidson English reads: Rabba bar Avuh says that Rav says]: actually it is Rabbi Yehuda; and why does it teach that she is not betrothed? Where the firstborn donkey is worth only a shekel, and Rabbi Yehuda holds like Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, as it is taught: “You shall redeem with a lamb”: you shall redeem immediately, even before thirty [days]; you shall redeem with any amount, that is, even with any lamb at all, worth only a zuz.
rashi:b27.2: “You shall redeem,” “you shall redeem”: it is written twice: “And every firstborn donkey you shall redeem with a lamb” (Exodus 13:13) [and again in Exodus 34:20].
gershom:b22.1: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says: there is no redemption for less than a shekel; and below it explains the reason. And since there is no redemption for less than a shekel, and the firstborn donkey is worth only a shekel, there is no difference, and she is not betrothed.
gershom:b23.1: The Master said: “You shall redeem,” etc.: obvious, for neither “from a month old” is written about it, nor is any value written for the lamb.
rashi:b29.1: It is juxtaposed with a firstborn of man: as it is written (Numbers 18:15), “The firstborn of man and the firstborn of the non-kosher animal you shall redeem.”
gershom:b24.1: It was necessary for the tanna to say this, since it is juxtaposed with a firstborn of man, as it is written: “But you shall surely redeem the firstborn of man, and the firstborn of the non-kosher animal you shall redeem.”
rashi:b29.2: Just as a firstborn of man: his redemption is after thirty days, “And their redemption money, from a month old you shall redeem,” and one must give five sela.
rashi:b29.3: So too here, after thirty days, and five: sela one must give.
gershom:b25.1: Just as a firstborn of man is after thirty: as it is written, “And their redemption, from a month old you shall redeem,” and five shekels is his redemption.
gershom:b26.1: All valuations: that is, every redemption that you redeem.
gershom:b27.1: And the Rabbis: that [verse], “And all your valuations shall be by the shekel,” is written about affordability; that is, a poor man who said, “The valuation of so-and-so is upon me”: if he can afford to give a shekel, he must give it to the priest, as it is written, “According to what the vower can afford”; and if he cannot afford to give a shekel, he is exempt, because it is stated, “And all your valuations shall be by the shekel.” And actually, regarding a firstborn donkey, “you shall redeem” with any amount.
